description: We want to bring knowledge to other young people, using science and technology.
summary:
We developed Travix 3D – Left Behind, Not Forgotten, a free, real-time 3D map of the Solar System that tells the stories of the hardware humanity left on the Moon, Mars and beyond. From the Apollo descent stages and Surveyor landers to Spirit, Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity, users find 54 missions at their real landing sites.

It addresses the challenge by giving every artifact its own story: what it was, what science it made possible, why it was left there and where it is today, linked to its official NASA source. Real NASA and JPL data drive the planet positions and 3D models.

Travix 3D is made for every age, from children and teenagers to adults and seniors, and each person chooses how to learn. They can follow narrated guided tours, fly freely, ask by voice ("take me to Mars"), watch how each mission landed, explore a space glossary or test themselves with a quiz.

It is important because it turns discarded equipment into a doorway to science for everyone. It works offline on ordinary phones and computers, in English and Spanish, so these lessons can reach classrooms, homes and communities with poor internet.
details:
Who we are

We are Steps Ahead, five people who had never met before the day of the event. Frank, a 13-year-old student, had the idea for the app. Juan José is a 21-year-old young man. Iván and Luz are a married couple of seniors. Luis Fernando is a teacher. Three generations sat at one table with one goal: to combine our own knowledge with AI tools and build the best possible way, today, to learn about the objects humanity left in space. We believe we achieved it, and the team itself became the proof of our main idea: if a child, a young adult, seniors and a teacher can build it together, all of them can learn with it.

What does it do and how does it work?

Travix 3D – Left Behind, Not Forgotten is an interactive, real-time 3D map of the Solar System that tells the stories of the hardware humanity left on the Moon, Mars and beyond. Users find each artifact at its real landing site. The collection covers 54 missions, including:

  • the Apollo descent stages, Lunar Roving Vehicles and ALSEP stations;
  • the Surveyor and Viking landers;
  • Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight and Ingenuity;
  • spacecraft such as Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer, Voyager, Kepler, Huygens and Rosetta/Philae.

Every artifact has a story card in four parts: what it did, why it mattered, why it was left there (an engineering decision or the end of its mission) and its legacy. Each card links to the official NASA/NSSDCA source. Each surface mission has a "How it landed" animation with sound, showing its real landing method: sky crane, airbags, retro-rockets or parachutes through Titan's haze.

Everyone chooses how to learn:

  • Explore freely: fly through space at your own pace, or turn on "ship mode" and travel with hyperspace jumps aboard our team's starship.
  • Be guided: follow 5 narrated guided tours, one of them a timeline of the hardware.
  • Just ask: a voice assistant flies you to any place you name ("take me to Mars").
  • Read the story: open any card and read or listen to it.
  • Learn the words: a 51-word bilingual space glossary (descent stage, RTG, sky crane, retroreflector…), with every word linked to its object in 3D.
  • Test yourself: 100 quiz questions that never repeat, each with an explanation and a jump to that place in 3D.
  • Get inspired: "Colombians at NASA" profiles 7 Colombian women and men who work on NASA missions.

The simulation runs in real time:

  • planet positions are computed from JPL Keplerian orbital elements (J2000), with IAU rotation models;
  • Earth's day and night side matches the current UTC time, and city lights glow on its night side;
  • the International Space Station flies over its real ground track, propagated from CelesTrak orbital data;
  • sunlight dims with distance from the Sun;
  • comets grow their coma and tails as they approach the Sun.

What benefits does it have?

  • For every age: short, clear texts for children; depth and real data for teenagers and adults; voice, narration and large controls for seniors.
  • Free and installable: it runs in any modern browser and installs as a Progressive Web App.
  • Works offline: after the first visit it needs no internet. All 3D models, textures and NASA photos are stored on the device.
  • Runs anywhere: phones, tablets and computers. It adapts its graphics to each device, so even low-end phones can use it; more powerful devices get sharper graphics and smoother motion.
  • Bilingual: English and Spanish, translated by hand, not by machine, so scientific terms are correct.
  • Accessible: it respects the "reduce motion" setting, supports keyboard navigation and offers voice narration.
  • Turns lists into stories: instead of reading a list of missions, people explore space and discover the stories themselves, which makes learning memorable.

What is the intended impact?

We want people of every age to see discarded space equipment not as junk but as a doorway to science. Each object left behind is a lesson in engineering, decision-making, perseverance and exploration, and a reminder of the people who made it possible. Our first audience is the public schools of Colombia, many of them rural, with little connectivity and few space-science materials in Spanish. We propose Travix 3D as a free resource for science and technology classes, starting with schools near our San Vicente venue. It is also built for families: a grandparent and a grandchild can explore it together. We also hope to encourage respect for these sites as part of humanity's shared heritage.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did we use?

Languages and frameworks: TypeScript, React 19, three.js (WebGL) with custom GLSL shaders for atmospheres, city lights, comet tails and the hyperspace effect, Vite, Tailwind CSS, vite-plugin-pwa (Workbox) for offline use, Web Workers for background image processing, the Web Audio API (all sounds are synthesized in code) and the Web Speech API (narration and voice commands).

Data and resources:

  • NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA) and NASA Science mission pages: mission facts, landing sites, dates and final status;
  • NASA 3D Resources: spacecraft models;
  • NASA Image and Video Library: mission photos with their NASA IDs;
  • JPL Solar System Dynamics: orbital elements;
  • CelesTrak: ISS orbital data.

AI tools, always directed and reviewed by the team:

  • the first version was generated with Google AI Studio (Gemini), and later development used Claude Code (Claude);
  • our team starship was created with AI: the image with Google Gemini and the 3D model with MakerWorld MakerLab "Image to 3D";
  • every fact was checked against NASA sources.

Development and hosting: GitHub for collaboration and Vercel for hosting.

Recommended hardware and software

Anyone can use Travix 3D on an everyday phone or computer. The app detects each device and adapts automatically, so smoothness and graphic detail improve or drop depending on the device's power:

  • Adaptive quality: on phones and devices with 4 GB of RAM or less, it renders at a lower resolution, uses lighter shadows and caps textures at 2048 px instead of 4096 px. On computers without a graphics card, it turns off shadows, glow effects and anti-aliasing so it keeps running.
  • What changes: on a powerful device you see sharper surfaces, softer shadows and fluid motion. On a modest one, everything still works and every story, tour and quiz is the same, with simpler graphics and some pauses when a detailed mission scene loads.

How is our project creative?

Travix 3D turns a catalog of abandoned equipment into a journey. Instead of a static list, users move through a living, real-time Solar System where every artifact sits at its true location. Several features make exploration feel like discovery:

  • the "How it landed" animations;
  • the "Nearby" panel, which shows the closest objects;
  • hyperspace jumps aboard our own starship;
  • the voice assistant;
  • narrated tours;
  • story cards and glossary words that link to one another, so a mention of Opportunity or Apollo 11 takes you there.

We combined scientific accuracy with storytelling. Poetic phrases are clearly labeled as interpretation, such as Opportunity's famous "My battery is low and it's getting dark", which interprets its last telemetry and is not a literal message. The app was also born in a creative way: the idea came from a 13-year-old, and the team learned to build it together across generations.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Every age: we tested ideas across our own team, from 13 years old to seniors, and designed several ways to learn so each person can choose their own path.
  • Accuracy: every date, landing site and mission fact was checked against NASA sources and is linked on each card. Positions, lighting and day/night follow real physics and real time.
  • Language and reading level: short, clear texts, a narrated welcome tutorial and two languages.
  • Connectivity and devices: offline support, careful memory optimization and graphics that adapt to each device, so it works on low-end phones as well as computers. We measured memory use in emulated phones and kept it under control, with no crashes.
  • Accessibility: reduced-motion support, keyboard navigation and optional narration.

    Try it and see the code
  • Live app: https://travix-3-d.vercel.app/ (free, no sign-up; works on phones and computers)
  • Source code: https://github.com/frankdavidspacex12-ctrl/Travix-3D

The full code is open on GitHub. The README explains how the app works, lists every NASA data source and resource, and describes how and where AI tools were used. The commit history records each change the team made.
